lead: A multilevel inverter builds its output from several small DC steps instead of jumping between two rails. With m levels in the phase voltage, each step is V<sub>dc</sub>/(m − 1), the output is a staircase close to a sine, and each device blocks only one step. Lower dv/dt, lower harmonics and lower device voltage are why medium-voltage drives, large solar inverters, STATCOMs and HVDC converters use it. The three classic families are diode-clamped, flying-capacitor and cascaded H-bridge inverters.
prereq: You need: the half-bridge leg from single-phase bridges and the stepped-wave idea from harmonic elimination.

blocks.text: A two-level leg gives a pole voltage of +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 or −V<sub>dc</sub>/2. Split the bus into m − 1 equal parts and the leg can stop at m levels, from +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 to −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 in steps of V<sub>dc</sub>/(m − 1). The line voltage is the difference of two pole voltages, so it has 2m − 1 levels.
ΔV = Vdc/(m − 1), line levels = 2m − 1 ΔV is the step in volts, Vdc the total bus voltage and m the number of pole-voltage levels.

Each switch in a clamped leg blocks only ΔV, so on a 3.3 kV bus each switch of a three-level leg blocks only 1.65 kV. A staircase with more steps has a lower THD and smaller voltage jumps, which spares motor insulation and long cables.

Diode-clamped (neutral-point-clamped, NPC). One bus is split by m − 1 capacitors, and diodes tie the inner switch nodes to the capacitor taps. In the three-level leg, S1 and S2 on give +V<sub>dc</sub>/2, S2 and S3 on give 0 (through a clamping diode to the midpoint), and S3 and S4 on give −V<sub>dc</sub>/2. S1 and S3 are complementary, as are S2 and S4.

Flying capacitor. Capacitors floating between the switch nodes replace the clamping diodes; their voltages must be kept balanced by choosing between redundant switch states. Cascaded H-bridge (CHB). Each phase is a series string of s full-bridge cells, each with its own isolated source (a transformer winding, a battery or a PV string). A cell gives +V<sub>cell</sub>, 0 or −V<sub>cell</sub>, so a phase has m = 2s + 1 levels and a peak of sV<sub>cell</sub>.

head: Per leg (phase), m levels
Diode-clamped
Flying capacitor
Cascaded H-bridge
rows: (m − 1)(m − 2)/2 flying, plus m − 1 on the bus

blocks.text: Level-shifted carrier PWM compares one sine with m − 1 stacked triangles; phase-shifted carriers are used for flying-capacitor and CHB cells so each cell switches equally. At low switching frequency, a staircase whose step angles are chosen by harmonic elimination removes s − 1 harmonics with s cells; nearest-level control rounds the reference to the nearest step and suits converters with many cells.

More levels cost more devices, gate drivers, capacitors and sensors. NPC needs control of the midpoint voltage, flying capacitors need voltage balancing, and CHB needs isolated sources, usually a phase-shifting transformer, whose shifted windings also cancel input-current harmonics. For a low-voltage single-phase inverter a two-level bridge is cheaper.

figure.caption: Left: one leg of the first worked example’s three-level NPC inverter on a 600 V bus; the clamping diodes tie the inner switch nodes to the midpoint O, so every switch blocks 300 V. Right: half a cycle of the second example’s three-cell staircase, whose step angles remove the 5th and 7th and give a 305.6 V fundamental.

spec.aria: A three-level neutral-point-clamped leg: two 300 volt capacitors in series, four switches S1 to S4 in series, and two clamping diodes from the capacitor midpoint to the nodes between S1 and S2 and between S3 and S4. A box lists the switch states. On the right, a seven-level staircase rising to 300 volts in steps at 11.5, 28.7 and 57.1 degrees, with its 305.6 volt fundamental sine.

examples.question: A three-level NPC inverter runs from V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V. Find (a) the step size and the voltage each switch blocks, (b) the pole and line voltage levels, and (c) the numbers of switches, clamping diodes and bus capacitors per leg, and what they become for a five-level leg on the same bus.
steps: (a) ΔV = V<sub>dc</sub>/(m − 1) = 600/2 = 300 V, so each switch blocks 300 V.
(b) Pole levels: +300 V, 0 and −300 V. Line levels: 2m − 1 = 5, namely +600, +300, 0, −300 and −600 V.
(c) Three-level leg: 4 switches, 2 clamping diodes, and the bus has 2 capacitors shared by all legs.
Five-level leg: ΔV = 600/4 = 150 V; 8 switches, (4)(3) = 12 clamping diodes and 4 bus capacitors; the line voltage has 9 levels.
examples.answer: Three-level: 300 V steps and blocking, pole levels ±300 V and 0, five line levels, 4 switches and 2 diodes per leg on a 2-capacitor bus. Five-level: 150 V, 8 switches, 12 diodes, 4 capacitors.

examples.question: A cascaded H-bridge phase has 3 cells of 100 V. It makes a staircase with switching angles α<sub>1</sub> = 11.5°, α<sub>2</sub> = 28.72°, α<sub>3</sub> = 57.11° (cell k switches to +100 V at α<sub>k</sub>). Find the number of levels, the peak voltage, b<sub>1</sub>, and show that the 5th and 7th are eliminated.
steps: Each cell gives a pulse of width 180° − 2α<sub>k</sub>, so b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>cell</sub>/nπ)(cos nα<sub>1</sub> + cos nα<sub>2</sub> + cos nα<sub>3</sub>), with 4V<sub>cell</sub>/π = 127.32 V.
The 3rd is not zero (b<sub>3</sub> = 4.1 V), but it cancels in the line voltage of a three-phase star; the next line harmonics are the 11th and 13th, at 1.1 V and 10.1 V.
examples.answer: 7 levels, 300 V peak, b<sub>1</sub> = 305.6 V; b<sub>5</sub> and b<sub>7</sub> are zero; the 11th and 13th are 1.1 V and 10.1 V.

traps: A phase with m levels gives a line voltage with 2m − 1 levels; do not use m for both.
Each switch of a clamped leg blocks V<sub>dc</sub>/(m − 1), not V<sub>dc</sub>.
The m − 1 bus capacitors of an NPC inverter are shared by all three legs; only the clamping diodes are counted per leg.
CHB cells need isolated sources; they cannot share one DC bus.
Neutral-point-clamped is the usual name of the three-level diode-clamped leg; higher-level legs are just called diode-clamped.

quiz.q: State the voltage step of an m-level inverter on a bus V<sub>dc</sub>.
Why does a pole voltage with m levels give a line voltage with 2m − 1 levels?
quiz.a: The line voltage is the difference of two pole voltages, which runs from +(m − 1) steps to −(m − 1) steps in single steps: 2m − 1 values.

quiz.q: A five-level diode-clamped inverter has V<sub>dc</sub> = 800 V. Find the step, the switch blocking voltage and the clamping diodes per leg.
quiz.a: Step = 800/4 = 200 V, each switch blocks 200 V, and (4)(3) = 12 clamping diodes per leg.

quiz.q: A CHB has 4 cells of 50 V per phase. Find the phase levels, the peak and the line levels.
quiz.a: m = 9 levels, peak 200 V, line levels 2 × 9 − 1 = 17.

quiz.q: Why does a CHB need isolated sources while an NPC can use one bus?
quiz.a: Cells in series sit at different potentials, so each needs its own floating source. The NPC leg clamps to taps of one capacitor string, all at fixed potentials of the same bus.

quiz.q: Give two benefits and two costs of more levels.
quiz.a: Benefits: smaller steps, lower dv/dt and THD; lower device voltage. Costs: more devices, drivers and capacitors; capacitor balancing and, for CHB, isolated sources.

beyond: Not for the exam. The modular multilevel converter (MMC) stacks hundreds of half-bridge submodules and is the standard HVDC converter; active NPC legs spread losses in three-level drives. Search for modular multilevel converter and ANPC inverter.
